idiom_name: class Adapter : ITarget with a private readonly adaptee field
implementation_notes: C# forbids multiple inheritance of classes, so the object adapter is the normal form: a class implements the target interface and holds the adaptee in a private readonly field (constructor injection), translating each member; explicit interface implementation is used when the adapter should expose the target contract only through the interface. The BCL contains examples of interface reshaping - StreamReader presents a Stream through TextReader, while DbDataAdapter supplies common DataAdapter and IDbDataAdapter behaviour for relational providers - and a pluggable-adapter variation can route calls through delegate fields so one adapter serves several adaptees or renames members at construction time. Primary constructors and target-typed new shorten the boilerplate but do not remove the hand-written delegation.
pitfalls: C# cannot inherit two classes, so a class adapter is impossible for a class adaptee - only the interface branch can be inherited.
Explicit interface implementation hides a member unless the adapter is used through ITarget; mixing explicit and implicit members makes the public surface inconsistent.

Registering an adapter as a singleton in DI while it wraps a scoped or disposable dependency (for example DbContext) creates a captive dependency and lifetime leak - match the adapter's lifetime to what it wraps.
Returning vendor DTOs or SDK exceptions unchanged re-leaks the dependency; map into your own types and into the target's declared error model.

variants.name: Pluggable adapter over delegate fields
variants.implementation_notes: The pluggable adapter keeps the target interface but routes every operation through delegate fields assigned in the constructor, so one adapter class can serve different adaptees - even ones whose member names differ from the target's, which is what clients that insist on their own terminology need. The trade is that the wiring becomes the adapter: the compiler can no longer prove that the assigned delegates mean what the target interface promises, so the assignments belong next to the interface implementation and deserve a test.
variants.idiom_name: Func<...>/Action<...> fields assigned in the constructor
pitfalls: Delegates are strongly typed and bind method groups at compile time, but a semantically wrong delegate can still compile and return incorrect data; keep the wiring next to the interface implementation and contract-test it.
The wiring code is the adapter - keep it next to the interface implementation and cover it with a contract test.
Captured closures keep their targets alive, so a delegate field can root an object that should already have been disposed.
